extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political sociology, policing, and modern British political history
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic account of how a 'law-and-order' panic was institutionalised into an 'exceptional' form of the state in Britain (late 1960s–early 1970s), identifying phases, mechanisms, and concrete legislative/police/intelligence examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase condensation of law-and-order panic
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement by which the 'law-and-order' panic becomes fully institutionalised as an 'exceptional' form of the state can be condensed into three closely connected phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three phases are (1) the state's overwhelming tendency to move in the direction of the law (comprehensive legislative tightening); (2) the mobilisation and routine employment of law-enforcement agencies as 'informal' control; (3) the ideological convergence of diverse issues at the 'violence' threshold. The chapter cites instances of each as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 — legislative escalation ('move in the direction of the law')
rubrics_metrics.description: An overwhelming tendency of the state to legislate comprehensively, culminating in the tightening of legal sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include: Emergency Powers Act (internment), the Misuse of Drugs Act (sentencing escalations), the Criminal Damage Act (broad offence of damage with high penalties), and the 1971 Immigration Act. The text stresses the 'staggering' comprehensiveness of supporting legislative activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 — mobilisation of law-enforcement as 'informal' control
rubrics_metrics.description: The extended, routine employment of police and other enforcement agencies to exercise informal forms of containment and repression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Obscene Publications Squad raids (e.g., Warhol's Flesh, Oz prosecutions), surveillance and raids on 'alternative' scenes, the expansion of specialised intelligence units, and police practices on the streets in 'colony' areas. The authors emphasise routine operational activity that functions alongside or beyond formal parliamentary oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 3 — ideological convergence at the 'violence' threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency for diverse political and social issues to be reframed ideologically as matters of 'violence' or potential insurgency, justifying exceptional measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links urban guerrilla imagery, international terrorism (P.L.O. hijacks, Black September), domestic groups (Angry Brigade), and Northern Ireland events (Bloody Sunday, Aldershot bombing) as feeding a politics that treats many issues through a 'violence' lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalisation of threats and legalisation of containment
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern in which every perceived threat to social order is criminalised while means of containment are legalised and elevated to the legal threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note how statutes and sentencing (e.g., life recommendations for 'aggravated damage', long terms for drug trafficking) subordinate protest tactics (squats, pickets, demonstrations) and extend criminal liability, thereby narrowing legitimate contestation space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of surveillance and intelligence coordination outside parliamentary control
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of centralised intelligence and surveillance structures (information co-ordination and record-keeping) that operate with limited parliamentary oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named examples: National Immigration Intelligence Unit, National Drugs Intelligence Unit, and a Home Office claim that such 'operational activities of the police' are 'not normally subject to Parliamentary control.' These are presented as mechanisms that normalise expanded surveillance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militarisation and counter-insurgency doctrine influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The penetration of counter-insurgency theory and low-intensity operations doctrine into domestic security thinking and practice, converting military models to internal control roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited works and actors include Brigadier Kitson's Low Intensity Operations and the Institute for the Study of Conflict; the chapter notes the collapsing of distinctions (subversion → insurgency → terrorism) and the importation of colonial techniques into metropolitan policing and army roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban guerrilla imagery as justificatory spiral
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhetorical and symbolic deployment of 'urban guerrilla' and terrorist imagery that both provokes and legitimates repressive preparedness at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transnational/urban guerrilla movements (Weathermen, Baader-Meinhof, Japanese Red Army), P.L.O. hijackings, and the claim that bringing political violence 'back home' supplies proof for heightened security measures and militarised responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of law to suppress labour and industrial militancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Deployment of legal mechanisms and courts to contain industrial action and to criminalise tactics (e.g., flying pickets), with subsequent legislation and prosecutions used to deter or punish organised labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented episodes include the Industrial Relations Court fines and committals, the outlawing of flying pickets (post-1971–73), conspiracy charges against pickets, and use of sequestration/fines against unions—shown as part of the broader law-and-order trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral panic and media/establishment mobilisation as enabling factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The mobilisation of middle-class moral outrage, press amplification, and establishment figures in legitimising repressive policy and law-and-order politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual examples: Mary Whitehouse and the National Viewers and Listeners Association, the Longford Committee, prominent journalists and MPs (e.g., William Deedes, Ronald Butt), and extensive publicity that transformed moral protest into mainstream political pressure supporting repression.
